transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-06-24
Start time: 2:00 PM PT
Duration: 47 min
Title: Benchmark report v1 — legal claims review (latency/$, competitor context, disclaimers)
Attendees: Soojin Lee, Ethan Wallace, Michael Grant, Sofia Mendes, Henry Cho, Naomi Feldman

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
Summary:
- Legal reviewed draft benchmark claims (landing page, PDF, blog) with focus on substantiation, comparative language, and required disclaimers.
- Team aligned to remove/soften absolute statements and ensure every chart and headline is scoped to specific models, regions, dates, and configs.
- Legal provided guidance on how to reference competitor baselines: allow high-level context with clear caveats; avoid naming competitors in headers unless data and methodology are fully reproducible and archived.
- Security flagged operational detail leakage risks in methodology appendices and CSV/JSON exports.

Topics:
- What is an acceptable “latency/$” claim and how to define it consistently
- Comparative statements ("X% better than", "fastest", "industry-leading")
- Required disclaimers and where they must appear (web, PDF, blog, enablement)
- Substantiation: what artifacts must be retained and who signs off
- Security redaction for public artifacts

Action items:
- Soojin: update copy + create a single “approved disclaimers” block for reuse across assets (due 6/25)
- Ethan: revise PDF captions + executive summary, remove 2–3 claims flagged by Legal (due 6/26)
- Henry: add interactive page banner + tooltip language for metric definitions (due 6/27)
- Michael/Sofia: send “disallowed phrasing” list + approved comparative language examples (due 6/25)
- Naomi: review methodology appendix for sensitive operational details and propose redactions (due 6/26)

Transcript

[00:00] Soojin Lee: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone. Purpose today is just to get Legal comfortable with the claims in the landing page, the PDF, and the blog. We’ve got the latest draft open. Michael, Sofia, you both have the doc?

[00:12] Michael Grant: Yep, I’m in the PDF draft and the landing page copy. I also have the “message house” pulled up.

[00:18] Sofia Mendes: Same. And I added comments in the Google doc version—some of them are probably a little… blunt.

[00:23] Ethan Wallace: Please be blunt now, not on launch day.

[00:26] Henry Cho: +1.

[00:28] Soojin Lee: Great. Let’s start with the top headline. Current headline reads: “The best latency per dollar in production LLM inference.” Michael, that’s probably a no.

[00:38] Michael Grant: Correct. “Best” is an absolute claim. You can do “measured latency per dollar on Redwood Inference across X models and Y regions” or “benchmarking latency/$ across…” but “the best” implies a market-wide comparison that we can substantiate across the full competitive set, continuously.

[00:57] Sofia Mendes: Also “in production” is squishy. If it means “production-shaped workload,” fine, but it reads like “we are best in everyone’s production.” That’s risky.

[01:07] Soojin Lee: Ok. So headline becomes more descriptive: “A benchmark of latency/$ across models and regions” plus a subhead that says it’s on Redwood.

[01:16] Ethan Wallace: We wanted something punchy, but yeah. What’s acceptable punchy?

[01:20] Sofia Mendes: “Latency/$ benchmarks for LLM inference (Redwood Inference)” is fine. Or “Inference economics benchmark: latency and cost efficiency across regions.”

[01:30] Michael Grant: The key is: do not imply “overall fastest” or “cheapest” without scoping.

[01:36] Soojin Lee: Got it.

[01:38] Henry Cho: For the metric, can we say “latency/$ is our primary metric” without saying it’s the best metric?

[01:45] Michael Grant: Yes. You can explain why you chose it, but avoid “the only metric that matters” or “the industry standard.”

[01:52] Soojin Lee: Ok. Next: this line in the hero: “Up to 2.1x better latency per dollar versus leading alternatives.” This is the one we’ve been debating.

[02:04] Sofia Mendes: That’s the biggest flag. “Versus leading alternatives” is a comparative claim. We need to answer: which alternatives, which configs, which date, what’s included/excluded, and do we retain the raw data.

[02:18] Michael Grant: If you want to keep a comparative statement, it has to be extremely specific: “In our test on [date range], on [model list], in [regions], with [prompt set], Redwood Hosted achieved up to X improvement vs [named baseline] under [same workload].” And then the methodology must show parity as much as possible.

[02:37] Ethan Wallace: The issue is we don’t want to name competitors in the hero anyway. But we do want a strong takeaway.

[02:44] Michael Grant: Then don’t compare in the hero. Keep competitor context inside the report with heavy caveats. Hero can focus on transparency: “reproducible methodology,” “download configs,” etc.

[02:56] Soojin Lee: So for web hero: remove that “2.1x vs alternatives” entirely.

[03:02] Sofia Mendes: Yes.

[03:03] Henry Cho: We can still highlight “latency/$ across regions” without saying “better.”

[03:08] Soojin Lee: Ok.

[03:10] Soojin Lee: On page section “Key findings,” we have bullets like “Redwood is fastest across NA and EU.”

[03:19] Michael Grant: Same issue. “Fastest” is absolute and unscoped. Also “across NA and EU” is too broad. Which regions? Which providers? Which models? If it means “within Redwood regions” then say “lowest p95 latency among the tested regions on Redwood” or “consistent p95 across regions.”

[03:39] Sofia Mendes: You can say “consistent” if you show variance and define “consistent” (e.g., spread across regions under same workload).

[03:48] Ethan Wallace: So we can say “regional consistency: smaller spread between p95 latency in us-east and eu-west under the same workload.”

[03:56] Sofia Mendes: That’s better.

[03:59] Soojin Lee: Ok. Next: charts. The PDF has a chart caption: “Redwood delivers industry-leading cost efficiency.” That’s also a no.

[04:08] Michael Grant: Yep. Change to “Measured cost efficiency (latency/$) in our benchmark.”

[04:14] Ethan Wallace: Understood.

[04:16] Naomi Feldman: Also, anything that reads like “guaranteed” should go. I saw one line: “predictable latency at scale.” It’s true-ish but if there’s no SLA on Hosted, it’s risky.

[04:28] Henry Cho: Hosted has best-effort, Dedicated has SLA.

[04:31] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. So make sure we don’t blur that. “Predictable” can be interpreted as contractual.

[04:37] Soojin Lee: Good catch. We’ll change to “designed for” or “built for” and reference Dedicated SLAs separately.

[04:44] Michael Grant: Yes, “designed to” is safer.

[04:47] Soojin Lee: Let’s talk disclaimers. What are must-haves and where do they need to show up?

[04:54] Michael Grant: Minimum disclaimer set:
- “Results are based on benchmarks run by Redwood Inference on [date range].”
- “Results vary by workload, hardware availability, and configuration.”
- “Model versions, quantization settings, and serving configs are specified in the methodology.”
- “Latency/$ is a composite metric; see definition.”
- If any competitor context is included: “Competitor results are based on publicly available information and/or our best-effort testing; may not represent optimal configurations.” Or, if that’s too strong, remove competitor numbers.

[05:25] Sofia Mendes: Also: “This is not a promise of performance for any specific customer deployment.” That line should be present at least in the PDF and landing page footer.

[05:33] Ethan Wallace: How prominent does it need to be? We don’t want a wall of legal text.

[05:38] Sofia Mendes: Not a wall, but it can’t be hidden. For web: a short banner near the table and a “Methodology & disclaimers” link adjacent to the headline. For PDF: footnote block on any page with charts, plus a methodology section.

[05:55] Soojin Lee: Henry, can we do a sticky disclaimer row above the interactive table?

[06:00] Henry Cho: Yes, a persistent banner, and tooltips for “latency/$” definition. We already have a tooltip component.

[06:06] Soojin Lee: Great.

[06:08] Michael Grant: Another item: be careful with “most cost-effective.” That’s equivalent to “cheapest” in practice.

[06:14] Soojin Lee: We’ll remove.

[06:16] Ethan Wallace: Methodology write-up includes caching and batching. We need to be explicit: caching enabled or not? People will ask.

[06:24] Henry Cho: Current methodology says: caching policy: prefix caching off by default; KV cache reuse is inherent; continuous batching enabled with a set max batch window.

[06:35] Sofia Mendes: That needs plain-English translation: “We did/did not enable cross-request caching.” Otherwise people think we juiced numbers.

[06:43] Soojin Lee: Good point.

[06:45] Michael Grant: Also disclaim that some features may be default vs tuned. If we tuned Redwood heavily but did not tune competitors, that’s a fairness problem. Better to avoid competitor comparisons.

[06:57] Soojin Lee: We’re leaning that way.

[07:00] Soojin Lee: There’s a section titled “Why Redwood wins.” It’s marketing-y but it includes lines like “We always choose the optimal kernel.” That’s not substantiable.

[07:10] Michael Grant: Yep. “Always” should go. “We select optimized kernels based on…” is fine. Avoid “always,” “guarantees,” “never.”

[07:22] Ethan Wallace: We can rewrite as “The runtime selects kernels based on model architecture and sequence length distribution.”

[07:28] Michael Grant: Exactly.

[07:30] Naomi Feldman: On security—there are a couple of places we mention “internal fleet autoscaler” and “capacity reservation IDs” in the appendix screenshots. Those cannot be public.

[07:40] Soojin Lee: That’s from an earlier screenshot. We can swap.

[07:44] Naomi Feldman: Also avoid naming internal service names like “BenchServe” or whatever. Keep it generic.

[07:50] Henry Cho: We’ll remove internal endpoints from diagrams.

[07:55] Soojin Lee: Ok, shifting to the blog draft. Intro paragraph says: “We tested the top open models and found Redwood is the fastest and cheapest way to run them.”

[08:06] Sofia Mendes: Two flags: “top” and “fastest and cheapest.”

[08:10] Michael Grant: Rewrite to: “We benchmarked a curated set of open models on Redwood across multiple regions and report latency, cost, and a composite latency/$ metric.”

[08:21] Ethan Wallace: That’s less spicy but safe.

[08:23] Soojin Lee: We can add “production-focused” and “reproducible.”

[08:27] Sofia Mendes: Yes.

[08:29] Soojin Lee: The blog also has a line: “Competitors hide their numbers; we publish ours.” That’s spicy.

[08:35] Michael Grant: That’s risky because it implies intent/misconduct. Don’t do that.

[08:40] Sofia Mendes: You can say “We’re publishing our methodology and configs to support reproducibility.” Don’t talk about what competitors do/don’t do.

[08:50] Ethan Wallace: Okay, I’ll remove.

[08:52] Henry Cho: On the interactive page, we planned to include a “Compare to” dropdown that would show competitor baselines. That’s now questionable.

[09:01] Michael Grant: I would recommend removing it for v1 unless you have parity testing and retention. Otherwise you’ll get dragged into argument about fairness and “why is X slower.”

[09:12] Soojin Lee: Agreed, we’ll keep competitor context in narrative only, if at all.

[09:18] Sofia Mendes: If narrative includes any numbers, it still counts. But if it’s qualitative like “these metrics vary across providers,” that’s fine.

[09:25] Soojin Lee: Understood.

[09:27] Soojin Lee: Let’s talk about substantiation standards. What do you need us to retain for each claim?

[09:34] Michael Grant: For any quantitative claim that is public:
1) Raw logs (timings, token counts) for the runs used.
2) Run manifests/configs (model version, region, hardware class, concurrency, warmup, caching/batching settings).
3) Data processing code version (git SHA) used to compute the metric.
4) The final dataset used for charts.
5) A sign-off record: who reviewed data validation.

[10:01] Sofia Mendes: And retain it per the policy. I think you have a retention policy doc—make sure it’s aligned.

[10:06] Henry Cho: We do. There’s a public benchmark data retention policy that says keep raw logs and derived dataset for at least 24 months, with access controls.

[10:14] Michael Grant: Great. Then link to that internally, and we can reference it in approval notes.

[10:20] Soojin Lee: For approval workflow, do we need Legal sign-off on the final PDF and landing page copy only, or also the enablement kit?

[10:28] Sofia Mendes: Anything that contains claims can create risk. Sales enablement definitely.

[10:33] Michael Grant: We can do a lighter review for enablement if it’s strictly derived from the approved message house and uses only approved phrases. But if AEs will use it externally, treat it as external.

[10:45] Soojin Lee: Ok. We’ll keep the enablement talk track aligned.

[10:50] Ethan Wallace: There’s a line in the PDF: “Our numbers are independently verified.” We don’t have independent verification.

[10:57] Michael Grant: Remove. That’s a hard no.

[11:00] Soojin Lee: Yep.

[11:02] Henry Cho: Another phrase: “statistically significant.” Are we doing statistical tests?

[11:07] Sofia Mendes: Unless you can defend it, don’t say it.

[11:10] Michael Grant: You can say “we repeated runs and report variability” but avoid formal statistical language unless it’s true.

[11:18] Soojin Lee: We have stability gates and reruns on variance, but not like p-values.

[11:23] Michael Grant: Then don’t say “statistically significant.”

[11:27] Soojin Lee: Ok.

[11:30] Naomi Feldman: On the redaction topic: be careful not to reveal region capacity constraints. There’s a paragraph that says “APAC was capacity constrained.” That invites questions.

[11:40] Ethan Wallace: That was in a draft footnote. We can remove.

[11:44] Naomi Feldman: You can say “region availability may vary.” That’s fine.

[11:49] Henry Cho: We already have “availability varies by region.”

[11:52] Soojin Lee: Great.

[11:54] Soojin Lee: Let’s go through the specific items you flagged, Sofia. I saw comments around “guarantees,” “best,” and “leading.”

[12:02] Sofia Mendes: Yep. Top list:
- Replace “fastest,” “best,” “leading,” “unmatched,” “guaranteed,” “always.”
- Avoid “cheaper” unless you specify “cost per 1M tokens in our test.”
- Avoid “enterprise-grade compliance” unless you specify which compliance (SOC 2 Type II, ISO, etc.) and it’s actually current.

[12:25] Soojin Lee: On compliance, we were going to mention SOC 2 and ISO anyway.

[12:29] Naomi Feldman: That’s fine if accurate. But keep it separate from benchmark performance claims.

[12:34] Sofia Mendes: Yes.

[12:36] Ethan Wallace: Another line: “No other platform offers this level of transparency.” That’s similar to competitor intent.

[12:44] Michael Grant: You can say “We’re publishing configs and methodology” without “no other.”

[12:50] Soojin Lee: Ok.

[12:52] Henry Cho: There’s a practical question: we want to say “reproducible.” Is that safe if the harness is internal?

[12:59] Sofia Mendes: “Reproducible” can mean “we can rerun it ourselves deterministically.” If you mean “you can reproduce it,” then you need to provide the harness or enough detail.

[13:09] Michael Grant: Safer language: “We provide detailed methodology and run configurations to support reproducibility.” That’s not promising that any third party can perfectly reproduce it.

[13:22] Soojin Lee: Good.

[13:24] Ethan Wallace: We also have a section “How to replicate in your environment” for prospects. That’s separate.

[13:30] Michael Grant: That can be fine as guidance, but it cannot imply we guarantee they’ll see the same numbers.

[13:36] Soojin Lee: Makes sense.

[13:38] Soojin Lee: Alright, let’s draft the exact disclaimer block. Michael, can you propose a concise version we can paste across assets?

[13:46] Michael Grant: Sure, something like:
“Benchmark results are based on tests run by Redwood Inference between [DATE] and [DATE] using the configurations described in the Methodology. Results may vary by workload, region, model version, and system configuration. This report is provided for informational purposes and does not constitute a performance guarantee or SLA.”

[14:08] Sofia Mendes: Add: “Latency/$ is a composite metric derived from observed latency and computed cost; see definition.”

[14:15] Henry Cho: We can include a link to “What is latency/$?”

[14:18] Soojin Lee: Perfect.

[14:20] Naomi Feldman: And on the public artifact page: “Public datasets exclude sensitive identifiers.” Not sure it’s required but it’s a nice reassurance.

[14:28] Michael Grant: That’s fine.

[14:30] Soojin Lee: Let’s also talk about what phrases Sales can’t say. AEs will say “Redwood is the fastest.” We need a disallowed list.

[14:39] Sofia Mendes: I’ll send a list. Examples: “#1,” “market-leading,” “guaranteed,” “proven best,” “always faster,” “always cheaper.”

[14:48] Michael Grant: And approved alternatives: “In our published benchmark,” “as measured,” “under the tested workload,” “results vary.”

[14:57] Soojin Lee: Great.

[15:00] Ethan Wallace: Quick question on “up to” statements. Like “up to 35% improvement.” Are those okay?

[15:06] Michael Grant: “Up to” is okay only if the max is real and you can substantiate it, and you also provide typical ranges or at least not be misleading. But “up to” often triggers scrutiny because it highlights the best-case.

[15:20] Sofia Mendes: If you do “up to,” include the distribution, like median improvement or show the chart that makes it obvious.

[15:28] Ethan Wallace: So better to avoid “up to” in hero and keep it in the report where it’s backed by charts.

[15:35] Michael Grant: Exactly.

[15:38] Soojin Lee: Cool.

[15:40] Henry Cho: There’s another subtlety: we used the term “latency/$” with a slash. Some people interpret as dollars per latency rather than latency per dollar. We need a clear definition.

[15:52] Soojin Lee: Right. We’ve been debating naming. The page will say “latency per dollar (higher is better)” or “cost efficiency (higher is better).”

[16:01] Sofia Mendes: “Cost efficiency (higher is better)” is safer. “Latency per dollar” is okay if defined.

[16:08] Michael Grant: Also make sure you don’t invert the meaning. If “higher is better,” say it.

[16:14] Henry Cho: We’ll add that in the UI.

[16:17] Soojin Lee: Ok.

[16:18] (crosstalk)

[16:20] Ethan Wallace: Sorry, one more: the PDF has a quote placeholder like “Redwood cut our inference bill in half.” If we get an actual customer quote, does Legal need to review it?

[16:30] Michael Grant: Yes, and you need customer written approval. And the quote must be accurate and not misleading; ideally tied to their specific workload.

[16:40] Soojin Lee: We have a quote tracker with approvals, we’ll route through Legal.

[16:45] Naomi Feldman: And make sure it doesn’t imply sharing customer data or specifics.

[16:50] Soojin Lee: Got it.

[16:52] Soojin Lee: Are there any “must remove” items that would block approval?

[16:56] Michael Grant: Yes:
- Remove “independently verified.”
- Remove absolute superlatives (best/fastest/cheapest) unless scoped and fully substantiated.
- Remove competitor callouts in headings/hero.
- Remove any claim implying an SLA for Hosted.

[17:16] Sofia Mendes: And don’t imply competitor intent like “they hide numbers.”

[17:20] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[17:22] Soojin Lee: Great. Anything else from security side, Naomi?

[17:26] Naomi Feldman: Just ensure public artifacts do not include:
- request IDs that correlate to internal logs,
- region capacity notes,
- instance types if they reveal supply agreements,
- internal service naming.
If you keep it at the metric and methodology level, you’re fine.

[17:46] Henry Cho: We’ll keep hardware class generic (e.g., “GPU class”) and not vendor SKU.

[17:52] Naomi Feldman: Perfect.

[17:54] Soojin Lee: Ok, I think we have the marching orders. I’ll consolidate an “approved claims + disallowed phrases” section into the enablement kit.

[18:03] Michael Grant: Send it to us before it goes out.

[18:05] Soojin Lee: Will do.

[18:07] Ethan Wallace: I’ll revise the PDF and blog copy today and tomorrow.

[18:10] Sofia Mendes: Great. Ping me if you want me to look at the revised hero text before you lock.

[18:15] Soojin Lee: Yes please.

[18:18] Soojin Lee: Recap next steps:
- Remove superlatives, competitor hero comparisons.
- Add disclaimer block in web/PDF/blog.
- Add latency/$ definition and “higher is better” language.
- Security redactions.

[18:32] Michael Grant: Sounds good.

[18:34] Soojin Lee: Alright, thanks all.

[18:36] Meeting ended (recording stopped)
